title: Instruction tuning and RLHF
story:
A base model predicts text. That is the whole of its training objective, and it is worth being precise about why it is not what you want: a plausible continuation of your question is often not an answer to it. The most likely text after a question, in a corpus of scraped pages, might be another question, or a list of related links, or a confident paragraph that is entirely wrong. Nothing in the objective distinguishes helpful from merely likely.

So write down what you actually want and optimise that instead. Try it for a minute and the difficulty becomes obvious. A helpful answer, an honest answer, a well-judged refusal — none of these can be written as a function of the output text. If you cannot write it down, you cannot differentiate it, and if you cannot differentiate it, gradient descent has nothing to work with.

The way out is to change what you ask a person for. You cannot say what makes an answer good, but you can look at two answers and say which is better. That judgement is cheap, it requires no expertise in the system, and it is available for exactly the cases where no rule exists.

Christiano, Leike and colleagues built that into a method in 2017, defining goals in terms of non-expert human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments. It solved complex tasks without access to the reward function, including simulated robot locomotion and arcade games, while providing feedback on less than one percent of the agent's interactions — a small amount of non-expert time, in the range of fifteen minutes to five hours, was enough to learn behaviours that are hard to specify at all. The mechanism is the useful part: comparisons train a model of the reward, and the learned reward model is what the system then optimises. An objective that could not be written has been fitted from examples of judgement.

Applied to language models in 2022 by Ouyang, Wu, Lowe and colleagues, the same idea has two stages. First, collect labeler demonstrations of the desired behaviour and fine-tune by supervised learning — show the model what a good answer looks like. Then collect rankings of model outputs and fine-tune further by reinforcement learning from human feedback — tell the model which of its own attempts were better.

Their premise is stated at the top of the paper and is the sentence this lesson exists for: making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user's intent. Large models can generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, or simply unhelpful — not aligned with their users.

And the result that proves it: outputs from the 1.3 billion parameter instruction-tuned model were preferred, in human evaluations on their prompt distribution, to outputs from the 175 billion parameter base model, despite having 100x fewer parameters. Truthfulness improved and toxic output fell, with minimal performance regressions on public datasets.

Read that number as an engineering fact about your own work. A hundredfold difference in parameters was outweighed by somebody specifying what a good answer looks like. When a model disappoints you, the reflex is to reach for a larger one, and this result says the cheaper question comes first: has anyone ever told this system what good means here? Most disappointing systems have never been told.

It also explains a piece of recent history that otherwise looks like magic. The public reaction to a chat assistant, as against the raw model that had existed for two years, was not caused by a new base model. It was caused by the alignment step — the same underlying capability, made to answer the question you asked.

Now the cost, which is where careless readings of this go wrong. You have not optimised for truth, or helpfulness, or goodness. You have optimised a learned model of what particular labelers preferred, under particular instructions, on a particular distribution of prompts. Every one of those is a choice someone made, and none of them is visible in the finished system. Aligned is a transitive word and the object matters: aligned to whom.

Two consequences follow from that, and both bite in practice. The proxy can be satisfied without the goal being met — an answer that is confident, fluent, agreeable and wrong scores well with a hurried rater, so optimising hard against the proxy teaches exactly that. And the authors say plainly that the models still make simple mistakes, which is the right note to end on. This step changed how models behave, it did not make them correct, and treating a preference-tuned answer as a checked one is the single most common mistake made with these systems.

problem.name: Learning an objective from comparisons
problem.shape: You know a good result when you see one and cannot write down what makes it good.
tell: the quality you want is obvious to a person and has no formula
the metric being optimised is a stand-in nobody actually cares about
outputs are fluent and confident and miss the point of the question
the reflex is to reach for a larger model before anyone has defined good
problem.move: Stop trying to write the objective. Collect judgements instead — demonstrations of what you want, then comparisons between outputs — fit a model to those judgements, and optimise against it. Then write down whose judgements they were, because that is now the objective.
problem.invariant: A comparison is cheaper to obtain than a criterion and is available in exactly the cases where no rule can be stated, which is what makes an unwritable objective fittable at all.
problem.breaks: What you optimise is a learned proxy for the preferences of particular raters under particular instructions, so the proxy can be satisfied while the goal is missed — a confident, fluent, agreeable and wrong answer scores well.

cost.time: human judgement is the slow input, which is why the sample efficiency of the method is the thing that made it practical
cost.space: the preferences are frozen into the model and the choices behind them are invisible in the finished system
cost.beats: hand-written rules and metrics, which cover only the cases somebody anticipated, and raw scale, which improves capability without improving intent-following

problem.practice: Take any system of your own that produces text or ranked results and try to write its quality criterion as a function. When you cannot, collect twenty pairs of outputs and mark which is better in each. The pairs will be easy and the function will be impossible, and that gap is the whole reason this method exists.

beats.broke: What you want from a model cannot be written as a function, so training optimised the only thing that could be — predicting the next piece of text, where plausible and helpful are not the same.
beats.fix: Collect judgements rather than criteria: demonstrations of good behaviour, then comparisons between outputs, fitted into a reward model that the system is optimised against.
beats.cost: The objective becomes a learned proxy for what particular raters preferred, so it can be satisfied without the goal being met and the models still make simple mistakes.

interview.answer:
Because a preference is a judgement, and people can give judgements they cannot justify as rules. I cannot write down what makes an answer helpful or honest — and what cannot be written cannot be differentiated, so gradient descent has nothing to optimise. But I can look at two answers and say which is better, in seconds, without expertise.

The 2017 work turned that into a method: goals defined by non-expert human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments, solving complex tasks without access to the reward function, with feedback on less than one percent of the agent's interactions and fifteen minutes to five hours of human time. On language models in 2022 it is two stages: labeler demonstrations for a supervised fine-tune, then rankings of the model's own outputs for reinforcement learning from human feedback. The premise was that making models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user's intent, and the result was that outputs from the 1.3 billion parameter tuned model were preferred to the 175 billion parameter base model despite 100x fewer parameters, with better truthfulness, less toxicity and minimal regressions.

What I am optimising afterwards is not truth or helpfulness. It is a learned model of what particular labelers preferred, under particular instructions, on a particular prompt distribution — aligned is transitive, and the object is those raters.

So the two failure modes I watch for are that the proxy can be satisfied while the goal is missed, since a confident, fluent, agreeable and wrong answer scores well with a hurried rater, and that none of this makes the model correct: the paper says plainly that simple mistakes remain.
